newsitem.title: USA: Black vote crucial to Democratic win in Louisiana.
newsitem.headline: Black vote crucial to Democratic win in Louisiana.

text.p: A solid turnout by black voters is the cornerstone of a Democratic victory in Louisiana's close and increasingly nasty U.S. Senate race, but that is far from a sure bet this year, analysts say.

The bitter racial fallout from a political grudge, coupled with the residue of warfare among state Democratic factions this fall, could cut enough votes from Democrats' traditional base to give Republicans their first Senate seat from Louisiana this century, political analysts told Reuters.

With less than a week left before the election, most analysts said the race between former State Treasurer Mary Landrieu, 40, a Democrat, and Republican state Representative Louis "Woody" Jenkins, 49, is a virtual dead heat. Most agree that Landrieu needs 90 percent of the state's black votes and 35 percent or more of the white votes to pull off a win.

"No one is sure what the blacks are going to do," said Ed Renwick, head of Loyola University's Institute of Politics. "If they don't turn out to vote for her, or skip voting on that race because of lingering animosity from last year's governor's race, it could put her in deep trouble."

A feud between Landrieu and U.S. Representative Cleo Fields, one of the state's two black congressmen, erupted just days before the 1995 primary when both were running for governor. Fields accused Landrieu of "playing the race card" by airing ads on black radio stations saying she was the only candidate who could beat Republican candidate Mike Foster.

After he won the primary, with a virtual lock on black voters, Fields lost overwhelmingly to Foster in the general election. Fields was furious with Landrieu for not closing Democratic ranks and endorsing him in that runoff.
Democratic Sen. John Breaux brokered a truce of sorts this month in which Landrieu expressed regret if she offended anyone during the 1995 campaign and Fields half-heartedly endorsed her Senate bid.

After Landrieu was booed two weeks ago at a unity rally led by Vice President Al Gore at predominantly black Southern University in Baton Rouge, Breaux acknowledged, "We still have a lot of work to do."

Republicans called New Orleans Mayor Marc Morial's request Tuesday for a Justice Department probe into possible links between Nicarauguan contras, drug smuggling into New Orleans black neighbourhoods and a charity run by Jenkins in Central America another effort to unite blacks behind Landrieu and a new political low.

Jenkins was livid. "It's a complete and total lie. Marc Morial and Mary Landrieu are willing to destroy another human being for their political gain. I've never used drugs, never been associated with drugs. The very idea..."

Jenkins campaign chairman Tony Perkins told Reuters, "What happened is just the depth of bad politics. It is unbelievable, disgusting, for a mayor to abuse his office this way for political ends. It's despicable."
A Landrieu spokesman said the candidate was not associated with Morial's position but was aware of it and did not discourage him from seeking an investigation.
